en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 65, the Bhaddāli Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I eat a single meal at a single sitting.”
“Monks, when I eat a single meal at one sitting, I experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling.
Come, monks, you too should eat a single meal at one sitting;
for when you eat a single meal at one sitting, monks, you too will experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling.”
When this was said, the Venerable Bhaddāli said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I am not able to eat at a single sitting;
for if I were to eat at a single sitting, venerable sir, there might be anxiety in me, there might be remorse.”
“In that case, Bhaddāli, wherever you are invited to eat, you should eat one portion and then take out another portion before eating.
In this way, Bhaddāli, while eating, you will be able to subsist on a single sitting.
“Even in this way, Bhante, I am not able to eat.”
“Even so, Bhante, as I eat, there would be anxiety for me; there would be remorse.
Then, while the Blessed One was laying down the training rule and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was undertaking the training, the Venerable Bhaddāli declared his lack of enthusiasm.
Then, throughout that entire three-month period, the Venerable Bhaddāli did not present himself before the Blessed One, as one who fails to fulfill the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were engaged in making robes for the Blessed One, thinking, "When his robes are finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour.
Then the Venerable Bhaddāli approached those bhikkhus; having approached, he exchanged greetings with them.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Bhaddāli was sitting there, those bhikkhus said to him:
"Friend Bhaddāli, this robe-making for the Blessed One is being carried out.
When his robes are finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour."
“Come now, friend Bhaddāli, attend closely to this fault so that it does not become even more difficult for you later.
“Very well, friends,” the Venerable Bhaddāli replied to those monks and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Bhaddāli said this to the Blessed One:

"A transgression, venerable sir, has overcome me—like that of a fool, like that of one who is deluded, like that of one who is unwholesome—in that when the Blessed One was proclaiming the training rule and the community of monks was undertaking the training, I voiced my lack of enthusiasm.
May the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of restraint in the future."

“Truly, Bhaddāli, a transgression has overcome you, as foolish, as deluded, and as unwholesome as it was, in that when the training rules were being proclaimed by me and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was undertaking the training, you expressed your lack of enthusiasm.
Furthermore, Bhaddāli, this circumstance had not been penetrated by you:
‘The Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī; the Blessed One will know me—’”
‘The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
This opportunity, Bhaddāli, was not recognized by you.
Furthermore, this opportunity, Bhaddāli, was not recognized by you:
‘Many bhikkhus have entered the rains residence at Sāvatthī;
they too will know me as the bhikkhu named Bhaddāli, who is not fulfilling the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
This, Bhaddāli, was another occasion that you had failed to penetrate.
Furthermore, Bhaddāli, you did not penetrate this fact:
"Many bhikkhunīs have entered the rains retreat at Sāvatthī;
they too will know me—that the bhikkhu named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation."
This opportunity, Bhaddāli, was not recognized by you.
This other opportunity, Bhaddāli, was also not recognized by you:
"There are many lay followers residing in Sāvatthī; they too will know me—"
‘The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
This opportunity, Bhaddāli, was not recognized by you.
Furthermore, this opportunity, Bhaddāli, was not recognized by you:
‘There are many female lay followers residing in Sāvatthī;
they too will know me as the bhikkhu named Bhaddāli, who is not fulfilling the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
This, Bhaddāli, was another opportunity that you failed to penetrate.
Furthermore, Bhaddāli, you failed to realize this:
"Many ascetics and brahmins of various sects have entered the rains retreat at Sāvatthī;
they too will know me as the bhikkhu named Bhaddāli, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, a certain elder bhikkhu who does not fulfill the training in the Teaching."
“This too, Bhaddāli, was an occasion that you had not yet penetrated.

“Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me—foolish as I was, deluded as I was, and unskilled as I was—in that when the Blessed One was proclaiming the training rules and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was undertaking the training, I expressed my lack of enthusiasm.
May the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression, for the sake of restraint in the future.”

“Truly, Bhaddāli, a transgression has overcome you, as foolish, as deluded, and as unwholesome as it was, in that when the training rules were being proclaimed by me and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was undertaking the training, you voiced your lack of enthusiasm.
What do you think, Bhaddāli?
Suppose there were a bhikkhu here who was liberated in both ways; to him I would speak thus:”
“Come, bhikkhu, be a bridge for me across the mud,” would he then cross over, or would he turn his body away from it, or would he say, “No, Bhante”?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“What do you think, Bhaddāli?”
In this case, a bhikkhu is one liberated by wisdom … a body-witness … one who has attained vision …
To one liberated by faith,
to a follower of the Dhamma,
or to a follower by faith, I would speak thus:
“Come, bhikkhu, be a stepping-stone for me in the mud. Would he then step onto it, or would he turn his body away from it, or would he say, “No, Bhante”?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“What do you think, Bhaddāli?”

“Bhaddāli, at that time, were you one liberated in both ways, or one liberated by wisdom, or a body-witness, or one attained to view, or one liberated by faith, or a Dhamma-follower, or a faith-follower?
“No, venerable sir.
“Then, Bhaddāli, at that time were you not empty, hollow, and fallen short?”
“So it is, Bhante.

A transgression has overcome me, Bhante—a transgression born of folly, delusion, and unwholesomeness—in that when the Blessed One was proclaiming the training rules and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was undertaking the training, I expressed my lack of enthusiasm.
May the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.”

“Truly, Bhaddāli, a transgression has overcome you, as befits one who is foolish, deluded, and unwholesome, in that when the training rules were being proclaimed by me and the community of monks was undertaking the training, you voiced your lack of enthusiasm.
But since you, Bhaddāli, having seen your transgression as a transgression, make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.

For this, Bhaddāli, is growth in the discipline of the Noble One: that one who sees a transgression as a transgression makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma and undertakes restraint for the future.”
“Here, Bhaddāli, a certain bhikkhu does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
It occurs to him:
‘What if I were to resort to a secluded lodging—a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, or an open space, or a heap of straw?’”
‘Perhaps I might realize a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
Thus, he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
While he dwells thus withdrawn, his teacher censures him; wise companions in the holy life, having investigated, also censure him; deities also censure him; and he himself censures himself.
Thus, being reproached by the Teacher, reproached by wise fellow-celibates who have investigated the matter,
reproached by deities, and reproaching himself, he does not realize any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
For what reason?
For it is thus, Bhaddāli, with one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.
But here, Bhaddāli, some bhikkhu fulfills the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.
It occurs to him thus:
‘What if I were to resort to a secluded lodging—a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, or an open space, or a heap of straw?
Perhaps I might realize for myself a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
Thus, he resorts to a secluded lodging—a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.

As he dwells thus withdrawn, neither the Teacher reproaches him, nor do wise fellow-practitioners reproach him after due investigation, nor do deities reproach him, nor does he himself reproach himself. Being unreproached by the Teacher,
unreproached by wise fellow-practitioners after due investigation,
unreproached by deities, and unreproached by himself, he realizes a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

Thus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
For what reason?
Because it is so, Bhaddāli, for one who fulfills the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.

Furthermore, Bhaddāli, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
For what reason?
Because it is so, Bhaddāli, for one who fulfills the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.
Furthermore, Bhaddāli, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in happiness.”
For what reason?
Because it is so, Bhaddāli, for one who fulfills the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.
Furthermore, Bhaddāli, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief...

With the subsiding of [mental] pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. For what reason?
Because it is thus, Bhaddāli, for one who fulfills the training in the Teacher’s instruction.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
For what reason is this?
For it is thus, Bhaddāli, that one becomes a fulfiller of the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn.
He understands beings as they pass away and reappear—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, having been possessed of misconduct of body... [as above] ...have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a hell realm;
but these worthy beings, having been possessed of good conduct of body... [as above] ...have reappeared in a happy destination, in a heavenly world."
Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans... [he] understands beings as faring according to their kamma.
For what reason?
Because it is so, Bhaddāli, for one who fulfills the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering";
he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
He understands as it really is: “These are the taints”; he understands as it really is: “This is the origin of the taints”; he understands as it really is:
“This is the cessation of the taints”; he understands as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.”
One understands it as it truly is.
For one who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, there arises the knowledge: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
For what reason?
Because it is so, Bhaddāli, for one who fulfills the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.”
When this was said, the Venerable Bhaddāli said to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some bhikkhus here treat another bhikkhu with persistent force?
And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some bhikkhus here do not treat another bhikkhu with such persistent force?”
“Here, Bhaddāli, a certain bhikkhu is one who repeatedly commits offenses and is full of transgressions.
When he is spoken to by the bhikkhus, he evades the point with something else, diverts the conversation to external matters, and displays anger, hatred, and resentment;
he does not conduct himself properly, does not lower his hair [in humility], and does not seek deliverance.”
It is appropriate; I do not say, ‘I will do whatever makes the Saṅgha pleased.
In that regard, Bhaddāli, it occurs to the bhikkhus:
‘Friends, this bhikkhu is one who repeatedly commits offenses, he is full of transgressions.’
Thus, when being addressed by the bhikkhus, he evades one point with another, diverts the conversation to external matters, displays anger, hatred, and resentment;
he does not conduct himself properly, does not show respect, and does not behave so as to bring about his own removal [from the offense];
he does not say, "I shall do whatever makes the Saṅgha satisfied."
"It would be good, venerable sirs, if you were to examine this bhikkhu in such a way that this legal issue of his is not settled so quickly.
Now, Bhaddāli, the bhikkhus examine that bhikkhu in such a way that this legal issue of his is not settled so quickly.
Furthermore, Bhaddāli, here a certain bhikkhu is one who repeatedly commits offenses and is full of transgressions.
Being thus addressed by the bhikkhus, he did not evade one question with another, nor did he divert the conversation to external matters;

he showed no anger, hatred, or resentment; he behaved properly, lowered his hair (in humility), and conducted himself in a way that would lead to his release, saying, "I shall do whatever makes the Saṅgha satisfied."
In this regard, Bhaddāli, it occurs to the monks:
“Friends, this monk is one who repeatedly commits offenses and is full of transgressions.
When he is spoken to by the monks, he does not evade one matter with another, nor does he divert the conversation to external topics, nor does he display anger.”
He manifests his fault and lack of confidence; he conducts himself properly, makes a clean breast of it, and conducts himself so as to reach the end of the matter, saying:
"I shall do whatever makes the Saṅgha satisfied.
"Venerable sirs, please examine this bhikkhu in such a way that this legal issue may be settled quickly."
In this way, Bhaddāli, the monks examine that bhikkhu in such a manner that this legal issue is quickly settled.
Here, Bhaddāli, a certain bhikkhu is one who commits offenses occasionally and is not prone to many offenses.
When he is spoken to by the monks, he evades one point with another, diverts the conversation to external matters, and displays anger.

He manifests ill will and resentment; he does not conduct himself properly, he does not behave with humility, he does not act in a way that leads to his release, and he does not say, "I shall do whatever makes the Saṅgha satisfied.
In this regard, Bhaddāli, the bhikkhus think thus:
“Friends, this bhikkhu is one who commits offenses unintentionally and rarely commits offenses.
When he is spoken to by the bhikkhus, he evades one point with another, diverts the conversation to external matters, displays anger, hatred, and resentment;
he does not behave properly, does not show respect, and does not seek resolution.”
"It is not proper for him to say, 'I will do whatever makes the Saṅgha pleased.
Rather, it would be good if the venerable ones were to examine this bhikkhu in such a way that this legal dispute of his is not settled so quickly.
Bhaddāli, when the bhikkhus examine that bhikkhu in such a manner, this legal dispute of his is not settled so quickly.
But here, Bhaddāli, a certain bhikkhu is one who rarely commits offenses and is mostly free from offenses.
When he is spoken to by the bhikkhus, he does not evade one thing with another, nor does he divert the conversation to external matters, nor does he manifest anger, hatred, or resentment;
he conducts himself properly, lowers his hair (in humility), and behaves in a way that leads to his deliverance.
‘I shall do whatever makes the Saṅgha pleased,’ he said.
In this regard, Bhaddāli, the bhikkhus think thus:
‘This venerable bhikkhu, friends, is one who rarely commits offenses and seldom falls into transgression.’”
Thus, when being addressed by the bhikkhus, he did not evade one question with another, nor did he divert the conversation to external matters;
he manifested neither anger, nor malice, nor resentment. He behaved properly, lowered his hair (in humility), and conducted himself in a way that led to his deliverance, saying:
"I shall do whatever makes the Saṅgha satisfied."
"It would be well, venerable friends, if you were to examine this bhikkhu in such a way that this legal issue of his might be settled very quickly.
Bhaddāli, when the bhikkhus examine that bhikkhu in such a way, this legal issue of his is settled very quickly.
Here, Bhaddāli, a certain bhikkhu proceeds with mere faith and mere affection.
In this regard, Bhaddāli, it occurs to the bhikkhus:
"Friends, this bhikkhu proceeds merely by means of faith and merely by means of affection.
If we were to repeatedly press him and cause him trouble—"
‘May he not even lose that mere measure of faith, that mere measure of affection.
Bhaddāli, it is just as if a man had only one eye, and his friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives would protect that one eye, thinking:
‘May he not even lose that one eye of his.’”
In the same way, Bhaddāli, here a certain bhikkhu proceeds with mere faith and mere affection.
In this regard, Bhaddāli, the bhikkhus think:
"Friends, this bhikkhu proceeds with mere faith and mere affection."
‘If we were to repeatedly subject this bhikkhu to disciplinary action,
he might even lose that mere measure of faith and that mere measure of affection [he has for us]. This, Bhaddāli,
is the cause, this is the reason why they here repeatedly subject a certain bhikkhu to disciplinary action.
“But this, Bhaddāli, is the cause, this is the reason why they do not here treat some bhikkhus by repeatedly pressing them.
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason why formerly there were fewer training rules and more bhikkhus remained established in higher knowledge?
But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why now there are more training rules and fewer bhikkhus remain established in higher knowledge?”
“It is so, Bhaddāli, that when beings are declining and the true Dhamma is disappearing, the training rules become more numerous while fewer bhikkhus remain established in higher knowledge.
But, Bhaddāli, the Teacher does not lay down a training rule for his disciples until certain things conducive to the arising of cankers appear here in the Saṅgha.”

But when, Bhaddāli, certain things that are bases for the taints appear here in the Saṅgha, then the Teacher lays down a training rule for his disciples for the purpose of warding off those very things that are bases for the taints.
Bhaddāli, as long as the Saṅgha has not attained greatness, certain things that are bases for the taints do not appear here in the Saṅgha.
But when the Saṅgha has attained greatness, Bhaddāli, then certain things that are bases for the taints appear here in the Saṅgha.
Then the Teacher lays down a training rule for his disciples for the sake of warding off those very things that are the bases for the taints.

But, Bhaddāli, as long as the Saṅgha has not attained the pinnacle of gain, the pinnacle of fame, the pinnacle of great learning, and the pinnacle of seniority, these certain things that are the bases for the taints do not appear here in the Saṅgha.
However, Bhaddāli, when the Saṅgha has attained seniority, then these certain things that are the bases for the taints appear here in the Saṅgha.
When these things become manifest in the Saṅgha, then the Teacher lays down a training rule for his disciples in order to ward off those very things that are the basis for the taints.
At that time, Bhaddāli, you were few in number when I taught you the Dhamma discourse on the simile of the well-bred stallion.
“Do you remember that, Bhaddāli?
“No, venerable sir.
“In that case, Bhaddāli, what reason do you give for it?”
“Indeed, Bhante, for a long time I have been one who failed to fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
“Bhaddāli, that is not the only cause, that is not the only condition.
Moreover, Bhaddāli, you have been known by me through long-term penetration of the mind with my own mind:”
“Moreover, this foolish man does not listen to the Dhamma with attention, with care, with his whole heart, and with an attentive ear while the Dhamma is being taught by me.
“However, Bhaddāli, I shall teach you a discourse on the Dhamma using the simile of a thoroughbred horse.
Listen to it and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Bhaddāli replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhaddāli, it is just as if a skilled horse-trainer, having obtained a noble thoroughbred horse, would first of all make it submit to the bit.”
While that bit is being applied to his mouth, there still arise in him certain contortions, writhings, and quiverings, as happens when a task previously unperformed is being performed.
Through repeated application and gradual application, he attains final peace in that state.
But, Bhaddāli, once the noble thoroughbred horse has attained final peace in that state through repeated and gradual application, the horse-trainer subjects him to further training for the yoke.

While that noble thoroughbred horse is being trained at the yoke-halter, there certainly arise certain contortions, writhings, and quiverings, as happens when a training never before undergone is being performed.
Through repeated training and gradual training, it attains final extinction (*parinibbāyati*) in that state.
Bhaddāli, when the noble thoroughbred horse has attained final extinction in that state through repeated training and gradual training, [it is said to be well-trained].
When it has become so, the horse-trainer subjects it to further training:
in the sequence of the circle, the prancing, the galloping, the dashing, the royal qualities, the royal lineage, the highest speed, the highest excellence as a horse, and the highest gentleness.

While it is being subjected to this training for the highest speed, the highest excellence as a horse, and the highest gentleness, there still arise in it certain quiverings, writhings, and struggles, just as they do when one is subjected to a training never performed before.
Thus, through constant training and gradual training, he attains final nibbāna at that very spot.
Bhaddāli, when a noble thoroughbred horse has attained final nibbāna at that spot through constant training and gradual training, the horse-trainer provides him with further grooming and water.
Bhaddāli, a noble thoroughbred horse endowed with these ten factors is worthy of a king, an accessory of a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, Bhaddāli, a bhikkhu endowed with ten qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
With which ten?
Here, Bhaddāli, a bhikkhu is endowed with the right view of one beyond training, and with the right intention of one beyond training.
He is endowed with right speech of one beyond training, he is endowed with right action of one beyond training,
he is endowed with right livelihood of one beyond training, he is endowed with right effort of one beyond training,
he is endowed with right mindfulness of one beyond training, and he is endowed with right concentration of one beyond training.

“He is endowed with right view that is beyond training; he is endowed with right intention that is beyond training; he is endowed with right speech that is beyond training; he is endowed with right action that is beyond training; he is endowed with right livelihood that is beyond training; he is endowed with right effort that is beyond training; he is endowed with right mindfulness that is beyond training; he is endowed with right concentration that is beyond training; he is endowed with right knowledge that is beyond training; he is endowed with right liberation that is beyond training.

Bhaddāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these ten qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Bhaddāli was uplifted and rejoiced in the words spoken by the Blessed One.
The Bhaddālisutta, the fifth, is finished.
